stories.title: Japan lawmakers visit China seeking to patch up ties
stories.summary: A Japanese delegation of lawmakers visited China in a bid to improve strained ties after PM Takaichi's Taiwan military intervention remarks angered Beijing. China had earlier responded with travel warnings and trade restrictions, affecting Japan's rare earth mineral supplies. Further visits and talks are planned, including by business groups and a former foreign minister, aiming to restore dialogue and cooperation. A delegation of Japanese lawmakers left for China on Aug 24 seeking to patch up ties in the wake of comments about Taiwan by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi that angered Beijing. Takaichi suggested in November 2025 that Japan could intervene militarily in any conflict over Taiwan, which Beijing insists is part of its territory. China warned its citizens against travel to Japan and imposed trade restrictions that have reportedly led to big drops in supplies of rare earth minerals to Japanese firms. The delegation comprises a member of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and two opposition lawmakers, all from a cross-party group that seeks to foster ties with China. They were expected to meet senior officials of the Chinese Communist Party, Japanese media reported, in the first such exchange since Takaichi’s comments. “In a situation where everything is currently cut off, I would like to make this an opportunity to somehow grasp an opportunity of dialogue,” said delegation member and Lower House MP Shinichi Isa, who is also public communications chief for the opposition Centrist Reform Alliance. An official from LDP Lower House member Gaku Hashimoto’s office confirmed to AFP news agency that he “departed (for Beijing) to stay for two days there”, declining to comment further. Japan’s top diplomat said in July he “discussed bilateral relations” with his Chinese counterpart on the sidelines of a regional foreign ministers’ meeting in Manila. Beijing’s foreign ministry spokesman later denied that a meeting took place.

stories.title: (2nd LD) PM vows zero tolerance for mishandling of missing person cases
stories.summary: Prime Minister Han Seong-sook pledged Monday to exercise zero tolerance and sternly punish whoever is found to have mishandled missing person cases, following revelations that a police officer closed cases without confirming the safety of those missing. Han made the remarks in a post on X, formerly known as Twitter, stressing that nothing is more important than the lives and safety of people and promising to overhaul the missing person investigation system and close any loopholes so as to ensure fair investigations. "We will thoroughly check if there have been unfair and unlawful acts by investigative agencies and issue stern punishment regardless of rank, based on the principle of zero tolerance," she said. "The government will pour in every possible effort to make sure missing person investigations are conducted strictly and fairly." Earlier in the day, Han ordered the National. Police Agency to look thoroughly into the handling of all missing person cases across the nation and pledged to overhaul the way police handle such cases, including separating the right to investigate cases from the right to close them. A police officer on the southern island of Jeju has been arrested for closing a missing person case without confirming the woman's safety. The body of Jang Mi-ran, 37, was found earlier Monday, more than three months after she was initially reported missing by her family. The officer was found to have closed another missing person case prematurely, and the man's body has been found. The prime minister said she feels indefinite responsibility over the case. "I pray from the bottom of my heart for the soul of the late Jang Mi-ran," she said. President Lee Jae Myung has also called for scrutiny of the police investigation system, expressing sorrow over the case, presidential spokesperson Kang Yu-jung said.

stories.title: Woman stranded in Spain after UK’s eVisa system mistakes her for twin sister
stories.summary: Nidia Webb, who is legally settled in UK, falls foul of ‘known issue’ with Home Office’s digitised immigration process A woman who is legally settled in the UK was left stranded at a Spanish airport after the Home Office’s post-Brexit visa system mixed her up with her twin sister. Nidia Webb fell foul of what she was told was a “known issue” with the eVisa, which was brought in as part of the government’s drive to digitise the UK’s immigration system but has faced problems that have caused concern for thousands of people. stories.title: My Arms Are Longer Now – comedy stealth game sends lawlessness into new territory
stories.summary: Developers who met through Australia’s improv scene and publishers of comedic party games have united for this slithering challenge in which you play as one extended limb Most stealth games cast you as a spy, an assassin or a master thief. My Arms Are Longer Now dispenses with most of the criminal person, to send in just one spectacularly badly behaved limb. It slithers across floors, winds around furniture, steals things and slaps anyone within reach – finally answering the question nobody asked: what if your own arm turned to crime? As Toot Games co-founder Matthew Jackson puts it: “You are the bad thing that happens to the people.” Continue reading...
